sources.label: Perez-Saez et al. 2022
sources.title: Cholera in sub-Saharan Africa
sources.description: For cholera in sub-Saharan Africa a second source fills part of that gap: the compilation behind Perez-Saez et al. (2022), from ministries of health, WHO, MSF, ProMED and ReliefWeb, marking the months when cholera ran above its usual local level.
sources.reference: Perez-Saez et al. (2022), Lancet Glob. Health 10, e831-e839, doi:10.1016/S2214-109X(22)00007-9

sources.label: WHO meningitis bulletins
sources.title: Meningitis
sources.description: For meningitis in the African meningitis belt, 2014 to 2026, the WHO West Africa weekly bulletins mark the months when at least one district crossed the WHO epidemic threshold; meningitis comes back every dry season, so only that threshold counts as an outbreak.
sources.reference: WHO Inter-country Support Team for West Africa, weekly meningitis bulletins, via MenAfriNet

sources.label: InfoDengue
sources.title: Chikungunya, Zika and dengue in Brazil
sources.description: For chikungunya, Zika and dengue in Brazil, InfoDengue (Codeço et al., 2018; Fiocruz and FGV with the Ministry of Health) marks the epidemic waves: months when municipalities above their own epidemic threshold held at least 3 per cent of Brazil's population (20 per cent for dengue, which never fully goes away). Chikungunya and Zika get one marker per state hit; dengue reaches nearly every state every summer, so it gets one marker per wave listing the states where most people lived above the threshold.

sources.label: DATASUS (SINAN)
sources.title: Leptospirosis, leishmaniasis and hantavirus in Brazil
sources.description: Also for Brazil, DATASUS (the national notification system, SINAN) gives leptospirosis, leishmaniasis and hantavirus by state and month; a month counts as an outbreak when a state's cases exceed the usual level for that month by four standard deviations, Brazil's own "control diagram" made strict, so that chance alone almost never trips it.
sources.reference: Ministério da Saúde, SINAN, via DATASUS (CC BY)

sources.label: WHO global dengue surveillance
sources.title: Dengue worldwide
sources.description: Dengue outside Brazil comes from WHO's global dengue surveillance (national cases by week or month, from 2007 in Asia and 2014 in the Americas), judged by the same rule on each country's national monthly total; months a country did not report are left out rather than counted as zero, and countries with fewer than five years of reports are not judged. The rule is strict, so an epidemic in a country whose other years were also high can go unmarked.

sources.label: WHO, PAHO and published reports (yellow fever)
sources.title: Yellow fever, dated reports
sources.description: Yellow fever is also dated from the reports behind Shearer et al. (2018): WHO's Weekly Epidemiological Record and outbreak news, PAHO bulletins and journal papers. A month is used only when a report states it or two sources agree; each marker links to its report.
sources.reference: Shearer et al. (2018), Lancet Glob. Health 6, e270-e278, and the reports linked from each marker

sources.label: WHO Disease Outbreak News
sources.title: WHO Disease Outbreak News
sources.description: Worldwide, WHO's Disease Outbreak News (as compiled by Torres Munguía et al., 2022) adds the outbreaks WHO reported, placed in the month of its first report, which is usually some weeks after the outbreak began. Reports about imported cases or overseas territories are left out where WHO's title says so, but a few imported cases remain, such as Ebola in Spain and the United States in 2014.
sources.reference: Torres Munguía et al. (2022), Sci. Data 9, 683, doi:10.6084/m9.figshare.17207183 (CC BY 4.0)
